The short version

Interactive Brokers gets paid by customers who trade and who keep money and securities there. They pay a commission when they trade. They pay smaller fees for market data and other services. The firm also earns net interest on the cash and the margin loans it carries. The charts are in dollars.

Net interest is the large line. Commissions are still compounding, and they rise with the number of accounts. Other fees are smaller. Principal transactions are what is left of the firm trading for its own book. That line was a loss in 2022. It is not the engine.

What is compounding now is the account base, the equity customers keep, commission dollars, and net interest. What looks mature is the price of a trade. Commission per cleared order has stayed in a narrow band. Before the filing renamed that row, the intensity was commission per DART, and that older figure is on its own chart. Profit on this page is income before income taxes, because that is the line the filings print.

The first quarter of 2015 was a pretax loss. It stays on the quarterly chart. The fourth quarters of 2011 through 2014 show the three-month column from the January letter. The fourth quarters of 2017 and 2018 show the pretax those letters printed.

Risks

  • The business breaks if customers take their trading somewhere else, or if the commission on each order collapses. The lines to watch are commissions, commission per cleared order, accounts, and daily trades.
  • Net interest is the large line. It moves when rates move, and when customers leave less cash on the books.
  • Most of the pretax profit does not belong to the publicly traded stock. Net income to common is the smaller line under pretax.
  • Orders sent through the firm's API are not a disclosed share. If that automated flow left, this page would not show it as its own number.

Close competitors

  • Charles Schwab. The large U.S. retail broker. Customers pay to trade, and the firm earns interest on their cash.
  • Fidelity. A private firm in the same retail brokerage and cash business.
  • Robinhood. An app broker. More of what it earns is payment for order flow and interest, and less of it is a desk for professional orders.
  • tastytrade. An options broker that also offers a way for software to send orders.
  • Alpaca. A broker built so developers can send orders through an API.

Open gaps

  • Free cash flow is not on the page.
  • There is no separate operating-income line; pretax is the profit line the filings print.
  • The fourth quarter of 2015 has no geography on the chart.
  • The six-way fee split is not printed for the fourth quarters of 2024 and 2025.
  • Commission per cleared order starts where the filing renamed the row; the older commission-per-DART figure is its own chart.
  • Other fees as one line are not printed before 2018.
  • Diluted weighted-average shares start at FY2008Q4 on the quarterly chart; earlier three-month prints are not on this page.
  • Trailing diluted EPS starts at FY2009Q3 (0.325), once four printed quarterly diluted EPS exist.
